anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model, indexing, partitioning and data-type choices do not fit workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths independent of statistics freshness.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or related log/temporary areas are close to or at space exhaustion, leading to allocation failures and blocked growth operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport and connection-handling layer cannot sustain the offered session or data-transfer rate, producing refused or stalled connections and socket-level waits.

When all three issues strike concurrently, the database shows a blend of symptoms: queries already slowed by full scans or non-covering index lookups take longer to return, holding server processes and network sockets open while large result sets dribble across congested links. Those prolonged sessions accumulate, inflating active connection counts until listener or OS socket queues overflow and new clients are rejected or time out. Meanwhile, the excessive I/O generated by the poor schema design (unnecessary table scans, row lookups, temp-space sorts) accelerates tablespace growth, temp-file inflation, and redo/undo generation, quickly consuming the remaining free space. Space shortages then cause auto-extend or log-archive stalls that freeze write operations mid-transaction; frozen backends remain connected, further saturating the limited connection pool and network backlog. Administrators may observe a mixed pattern of slow queries, intermittent "out of space" errors, rising waits on client read/write events, and periodic connection storms that mask which layer is primary.

Causally, inefficient schema design drives higher disk and temp usage as well as larger result sets, pushing the storage subsystem toward capacity limits. The same inefficiency prolongs statement execution times, increasing the duration each backend holds a network socket, which magnifies the impact of pre-existing network constraints. As space becomes scarce, allocation failures pause or abort writes; these partial or hung transactions keep locks and connections open, creating more network pressure and client retries. Retried connections and replayed workloads then amplify both space consumption (duplicate writes, additional temp objects) and connection demand, creating a reinforcing loop that rapidly degrades overall availability.

entry.official_definition: Sets the interval between optional checks that the client is still connected while running queries.
entry.trigger_condition: During a long-running query, PostgreSQL polls the socket at this interval and can detect a closed connection sooner.
entry.workload_impact: Long-running queries can be aborted sooner after the kernel reports that the client connection is closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, disabling connection checks.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
